If any person, officer or agent shall neglect or refuse, on demand of the Assessor or his Deputy, to give, under oath or affirmation, the statement required by this section, the Assessor or his Deputy shall make a minute of such refusal or neglect under his name, and an estimate of the taxable property which such person, officer or agent neglected or refused to so render; and the value so fixed shall not be reduced by the Board of Equalization. If the name of any absent owner of property is known to the Assessor, the property shall be assessed in his, her or their names; if unknown to the Assessor, the same shall be assessed to unknown owners. The form of the Assessment Roll, and the manner of making the assessment hereby ordained, shall be substantially the same as that prescribed by law for the purpose of taxation. In carrying out the provisions of this section the Assessor and his Deputy shall have power and authority to administer all oaths and affirmations authorized by law.

SEC. 4. On or before the FIRST Monday in August, 1870, and each year thereafter, the City Assessor shall complete his tax list or assessment roll, and attach his certificate thereto, which certificate shall be by him subscribed and sworn to, and substantially in the following form, to wit: I do solemnly swear that I have made diligent inquiry into the names of all taxable inhabitants of Hamilton City; that I have diligently investigated and ascertained the description, value, and ownership, of all taxable property in said city; that I have in all cases sought and put down the true owner, true description and true value of all PROPERTY assessed to the best of my ability; and that the annexed is a true and correct assessment roll, made in accordance with the laws of the State and the ordinances of the said city, and shall deliver said assessment roll, maps, books and the original list of property to the City Clerk, who shall immediately give notice of the same, specifying the time of meeting of the Board of Equalization by publication in some newspaper published in said city, or in such other manner as the Board of Trustees may direct; and shall keep the roll open for public inspection.

SEC. 5. The Board of Trustees shall constitute the Board of Equalization, and a majority of the Board, with the President of the Board, shall be a quorum for the Board of Equalization and the decision, a majority of such quorum shall be final. The City Clerk shall be the Clerk of the Board of Equalization. The Board shall meet on the first Monday after the completion of the assessment roll, and shall continue in Session from time to time, until the business of equalization brought before them is disposed of; provided, that no complaint on account of the assessment of any property shall be considered unless it shall be filed in writing with the Clerk of the Board within one week after the session of the Board commences. The Board of Equalization shall have the power to determine all complaints in regard to the assessment value of any property and may change and correct any valuation, either by adding thereto or deducting therefrom, if they deem the sum fixed by the assessment roll too small or too great; whether such sum be fixed by the owner or the Assessor, except that in cases where the person complaining of the assessment has refused to give the Assessor his list under oath or affirmation, as required by this ordinance, no reduction shall be made by the Board of Equalization in the assessment made by the Assessor. If the Board of Equalization shall find it necessary to add to the assessed value of any property on the assessment roll, they shall direct their clerk to give notice to the persons interested by notice deposited in the postoffice, directed to such person, naming the day when they will act in that case, and giving reasonable time to appear. During the sessions of the Board of Equalization the Assessor shall be present, and also his deputy, if necessary, as a witness in any case; and they shall have a right to make any statement, or produce any testimony pertinent to any matters coming before the Board. The Board shall make use of all the information they can gain from the county records, or otherwise, in equalizing the assessment roll, and may order the Assessor to enter upon the said roll any mortgage or lien, or other property that has not been assessed; and the assessment and equalization so made shall have the same force and effect as if made by the Assessor before the delivery of the assessment roll by him to the City Clerk.

SEC. 6. As soon as the equalization is completed the Clerk shall prepare a duplicate assessment roll, which shall contain the assessment as originally made and as equalized by the Board and to which shall be added a column showing the amount of taxes due from each part assessed, which duplicate assessment roll he shall certify to be correct, and deliver the same to the City Marshal, charging him with the whole amount of taxes shown to be due thereon. When the duplicate assessment roll has been delivered to the City Marshal, he shall cause notice thereof to be published in some newspaper published in the city, if there be one, to one week, requiring taxpayers to come forward and pay their taxes within four weeks from the publication of said notice. The Marshal shall immediately upon the receipt of the said duplicate assessment roll, commence the collection of taxes, and for that purpose he shall remain in his Office from 9 O'Clock a.m. to 4 O'Clock p.m. each day, for four weeks after the assessment roll has been so delivered.

It shall be the duty of the Marshal to pay over to the City Treasurer, on each Saturday after he commences the collection of taxes, the whole amount collected during the week proceeding, less his commissions for collecting, and to take duplicate receipts therefor—one of which he shall file with the Clerk, and the other retain as his voucher. The Clerk shall credit the Marshal on the assessment roll with all sums paid. The Iowa State University.

The Joint Committee Of the Legislature, appointed to visit the State University at Iowa City, made their report on Tuesday. We copy what they have to say on two or three points:

THE CO-EDUCATION OF THE SEXES.

It is well known that the University opens its doors on equal terms to both sexes; and in every class excepting in the Law Department, both were represented; and it is no disparagement to the young men to say, that, in every instance which came under the observation of the committee, the young ladies exhibited at least equal proficiency and aptitude in the studies pursued, and acquitted themselves with equal credit in all, not excepting the fine rhetorical exercises by the Senior class, which the committee had the pleasure of attending in the chapel on Friday afternoon. The general influence and results of the co-education of the sexes as it exists in this institution, are very satisfactory and go far to demonstrate the wisdom and expediency of the principle. The presence of the young ladies is constant stimulus as well as a constant restraint to the young men—bringing out the finer and nobler elements of character, and repressing the mischievous and sometimes vicious tendencies developed in institutions of learning where only the male sex is admitted. The young ladies are likewise benefited by the enjoyment of the equal privileges to which they are entitled, leading to broader culture, more correct views of life, and preparing them for the highest walks of usefulness.

THE STUDENTS.

"The committee were also gratified with the deportment and appearance of the students as observed by them and as reported by the faculty and citizens of Iowa City. No case of serious discipline has occurred for months, nor is there any complaint on the part of citizens as to boisterous or other improper conduct by the students. Many of the young men were soldiers in the late war, and are now completing courses of study which would have ended years ago had they not been interrupted by the higher claims of patriotism. The students, as a whole, seem to be pursuing their studies with commendable zeal, and lively appreciation of the advantages afforded by the University.

"The foregoing remarks, though general, may be applied more particularly to the collegiate and normal departments; and it will not be improper perhaps to speak briefly of those more recently established.

THE LAW AND MEDICAL DEPARTMENT.

"The Law department which has been in operation for a year and a half is meeting with substantial encouragement, and is discharging its functions in very satisfactory manner. It has added new strength to the University by widening the sphere of its influences and usefulness, and by increasing the number of its active friends; and promises in the future to add to its prosperity and renown.

"With reference to the Medical department, the committee, with due deference to the different opinions of others, are constrained to say that, in the judgment of the committee, its establishment at the present time is premature. One of the chief obstacles in the way of its successful operation is the want of suitable building for its accommodation. The rooms now being fitted up for this purpose, besides being small and very inadequate to the demand of such a department, are in the same building that is now, and must be for some time to come, occupied by the Normal department, and by other recitation rooms and society halls. Under such circumstances the difficulties in the way, especially in the practical study and demonstration of Anatomy, an indispensable branch of medical education, are readily apparent. If to these be added the almost total lack of facilities for clinical and hospital instruction, the obstacles in the path of the successful and satisfactory workings of this new department must be recognized as quite formidable, to say the least. Should the future demonstrate that the committee are mistaken in their judgment on this point, they will gladly recognize their error and rejoice with others in unexpected prosperity, as this criticism is made only in obedience to an imperative sense of duty.

ure your credentials as envoy extraordinary

lic of Chile. It will be an agreeable duty

been imported from France and are OF the most
elaborate and costly style. In one OF the salons is
a splendid portrait OF the Czar Alexander, painted
from life BY a Russian painter OF great ability.

The Question Of Rank Among Naval Officers.
The Secretary OF the Navy has notified the chair-
man OF the House Committee on Naval Affairs that
before the next meeting OF the committee a week
hence, he will furnish the report OF the BOARD OF
Officers appointed to settle the difficulties between
the line and the staff together with some suggestions
OF his own upon that vexed question. When this re-
port is before them the committee will take up
the whole subject and endeavor to prepare mea-
sures which will meet the case. The chairman OF
the committee, Judge Scofield, says he has no
feeling personally, either for or against the staff
officers. He does not think that the line officers
should have any more favors shown them than the
staff officers. He will oppose all measures however,
the tendency OF which is subversive OF good order
and discipline in the navy. The bill introduced yes-
terday BY Mr. Stevens, OF New Hampshire, is re-
garded BY the committee not only hostile to the
line officers but wholly in the interest OF that por-
tion OF the staff known as the Medical Corps.
It is believed to have been drawn by a surgeon OF
the navy who was formerly chief OF the Bureau Of
Medicine and Surgery.

Annexation Of British Columbia In Settlement
OF the Alabama Claims.

Senator Corbett's resolution about the annexation
OF British Columbia in partial satisfaction OF the
Alabama claims has opened up a subject for con-
sideration which, generally speaking, is being treated
in a very favorable manner. It is remarkable that

it is feasible to get not only British Columbia, but all
British North America as a quid pro quo in settle-
ment OF our claims against England, growing out
OF the damage done to our commerce by the cruisers
and corsairs OF pernicious Albion. What is still
more remarkable is the fact that England seems not
all too this mode OF adjusting the long pend-
ing and threatening difficulty occasioned by the
ravages OF the pirate Alabama. Yesterday after-
noon, when the attention OF Mr. Thornton, the
British Minister, was called to the subject instead
of treating it with ridicule or contempt, an impos-
sible concession On the part OF England, he gravely
remarked:

"Well, we should be glad to have the American
government agree upon the items OF its bill OF
damages against her Majesty's government. Up to
the present time the United States has confined
itself to the boldest generalities. We could not
comprehend accurately what the American govern-
ment required in the way OF settlement; if it would
only say precisely what is needed, we can soon
come to a DECISION. Let it be a bill OF items and
present it, and we will consider it with due respect."

From the manner in which these remarks were
made, the gentleman to whom they were addressed
inferred that Mr. Thornton meant that should our
government ask for all OF British North America,
England would not interpose any serious objection.
This little fact may be OF some use to Sumner and
his colleagues in arranging their small bill against
England.

Another Defalcation Discovered.

It is alleged here at the Treasury Department that
the superintendent OF a certain assay office is de-
faulter to the tune OF $4,000. The accused, it is
stated, up on plea that he was swindled out OF
a large amount OF money by a special agent OF the
Treasury Department, former pet OF ex-Secretary
Chase, who obtained $1,000 from him on false pre-
tenses and afterwards other sums, amounting alto-
gether to $4,000. The remaining $4,000 is not
accounted for. It is understood that the accused
will be removed BY the Secretary OF the Treasury
and prosecuted.

The Sacs and Foxes on Their Reservation.

The following letter was received at the office OF
the superintendent OF Indian Affairs:

LAWRENCE, Kansas, Jan. 4, 1870.
Hon. E. S. PARKER, Commissioner OF Indian Af-
fairs.

SIR—In a letter from Agent Miller, OF the Sacs and
Foxes dated on their new reservation, Indian Terr-
itory, ON the 10th ult., I am informed they arrived
the 18th, with the exception OF a few ox teams,
which were close behind. A snow storm commenced
on the day OF their arrival. There was some sick-
ness en route from ague, and TWO deaths, one from
consumption and one boy, from it. Both
received the kind care OF the agent,
yet located the agency, travelling being obstructed
by snow, but the prospects were good. Health
among the Indians was pretty good. Their arrival
at their new homes was at an unpropitious time
in consequence OF the deep snow, but the agent felt
encouraged that in a few days they would be in
more comfortable quarters.

Respectfully, &C., ENOCH HOAG,

Superintendent OF Indian Affairs.

Under the treaty stipulations the Sacs and Fox
Indians OF Mississippi residing in Kansas, agreed
to give up their homes and remove to the Indian
Territory, where a reserve was selected for that
purpose.

In reply to frequent inquiries made by local rev-
enue officers and others, the Commissioner OF Internal
Revenue DECREES that persons engaged in the business
of purchasing leaf tobacco, which they consign
to commission house agents or other persons to be
sold ON their account, are liable to pay the special
tax of twenty three dollars as dealers in leaf to-
bacco under the provisions OF the fifth ninth section
OF the act Of July 10, 1868, and that the liability is
incurred, notwithstanding the sales are made
through the agency of persons or firms who have
themselves paid special tax as dealers IN leaf tobac-
co.

Now that King William has set down with
his army to invest Paris, it becomes matter
of interest to inquire how his long communi-
cations are to be kept open. The siege may
be long one, for the French army inside is
fighting in its last ditch and hopes everything
from time; and the Notifications of the city,
even in the weakest point, are formidable
enough to suggest the slower mode of reduc-
ing them by mines and parallels approaches
rather than the more precarious and bloody
mode of storm and bombardment. King
Williams army, therefore, if the siege is pro-
tracted, will require food, ammunition, cloth
ing, medicines, and the other necessities of
an army, and he must look to his communi-
cations for the means of supplying them.


The main line of communication open at
present is the great Srasburg Railroad,
which runs from the Prussian camp at Paris
to Strasburg, through Chalons, Baf-le Duo,
Nancy, and Luneville to the Rhine, andwhich
is held by the Prussians almost throughout
its entire route. At Nancy, however, it con-
meets with another railroad running northeast.
through Metz and Saarbruck, into Prussia.
and by connections to Ooblentz and Mayence.
At Metz the Prussians have been busy build
ing a branch road running round the fortress.
so that there need be no breaking of bulk
from the heart of Germany to the besieging
army at Paris. This is the route over which
King William transports the supplies for his
army, a distance of about two hundred and
seventy miles, in the enemy's country.


So far we have heard of no determined
efforts to cut off his supplies by breaking up
this line. Prussian troops in strong detach-
ments from the besieging armies at Toul and
Metz hold the important positions on the
eastern end of the line, and other detach-
ments, probably from the main army before
Paris, preserve the westerly portion intact
These are doubtless able to beat off any
cavalry attack that may be made upon them,

The physiologist Blumenbach has made a graphic sketch of the process of senescence. He says that senescence is the longest and noblest speech of life, when nature is at its highest phase. The bodily functions are not so regular, and that something stops, as it is seen in each stage of this process. Then occurs the cessation of the senses, and the body begins to fail. Then the extremities grow cold, the eyes grow dull, the pulse becomes low and small, sometimes intermittent. Next the breath stops, stops and returns, stops, then with one long forcible expiration.

Mr. L. N. Yerger returned to this city yesterday morning, and voluntarily surrendered himself to Sheriff Lake. He has of no time since his escape, II week ago, been more than eight miles distant from here. He addressed the following to Gov. Alcorn:

STRASBURG, September 7.—On Tuesday
afternoon the joyful sight of a white flag
was beheld flying from the cathedral. This
was received by the same welcome token of
surrender from the citadel. The firing
instantly ceased, and a universal cheer arose
from one portion of the besieging lines and
was soon caught up and echoed throughout
the entire army.

The scene which followed was indescribable.
Excited officers embraced each other,
clasping hands. The men followed their
example, and some actually cried for joy.
The terms of capitulation, as agreed upon,
have already been reported.

I was fortunate enough to enter
the city with a Baden regiment. The sight,
which was impressive and sad, at the same
time was relieved by the evident joy of the
citizens at their release from their terrible
condition of suffering and suspense.

The commanders of the two forces, Gen-
eral Werder and Ulrich, met for the first
time yesterday, after the terms of capitula-
tion had been arranged. The meeting took
place just inside the gate on the east side.
General Ulrich advanced to General Werder,
and, with voice much agitated, said:
"I have yielded to an irresistible force
when further resistance was only reckless
sacrifice of the lives of brave men. I have
the consolation of knowing that I have"

General Werder was much affected. He
placed both hands on General Ulrich's
shoulders and said:
"You fought bravely. You will have as
much honor from the enemy as you can have
from your own countrymen."

All arms were surrendered except the
officers' side arms.

A hasty examination of portions of the
city shows that it has not suffered as much
as was supposed. The exterior of the cathe-
dral appears much injured, but not sufficient
to prevent its restoration to its original
shape.

Some five houses in place of cathedral are
burned here and there. The ruins of the
buildings show the danger to which the city
has been exposed. In the vicinity of the
cathedral on the east side of the city, the de-
struction was the greatest.

A singular appearance was presented by
the inhabitants busily engaged in removing
straw, bags, rags, mattresses, and every
conceivable means of stopping unwelcome
visitors from the windows. These defenses
were scattered in the streets, and gave the
appearance of general removal of the in-
habitants.

The ruins of the theatre presented a dis-
mal appearance.

Among the buildings destroyed was fine
public library. I am informed the books
were previously removed, or at least those of
the greatest value.

It does not appear that there had been
much actual suffering for want of food.
Their means were husbanded with the
greatest care. The principal cause of anx-
iety was confined to want of good water.

Several cases of mortality are reported as
the effects of the bombardment, but I am
inclined to believe that accidents are exag-
gerated.

One family, consisting of a father, two
daughters, two young sons and an infant,
had taken refuge in the cellar of their house
when the residence was struck by shell
and all were destroyed.

One old gentleman, a business merchant
in Strasburg for many years, informed me
that his daughter was killed in the streets.

The general feeling of the people is one
of great thankfulness for the capitulation.

Reports that are spread, charging Ulrich
with brutality are destitute of foundation.
His conduct toward the citizens was marked
with the greatest humanity and considera-
tion.

By the courtesy of proprietors of factories and railroad agents we have been enabled to procure interesting figures, giving an idea of the magnitude of the business. We will speak first of the business in a general way.

The business of dairying in this section of the Union increases from year to year, in a wonderful manner. It is but a few years since the idea that our lands would not furnish proper food for dairy stock has been disproved, and each season shows the wisdom of our agriculturists in persistently adhering to their belief in its future and certain value as a sure road to competence and wealth. In the face of frauds (such as changing the brands of cheese in Chicago markets), encouragement, sneers, and unjust discrimination, they have persevered, until now, Illinois butter and cheese are recognized as staple articles. This result is peculiarly gratifying to all who are interested in the development of our industries.

It is now admitted that the tract of country embracing the northern portions of Cook, DuPage, Kane, McHenry, Boone and Winnebago Counties is equal to any similarly sized tract in the Union for the purpose of dairying. The high, rolling ground, arability of soil and accessibility to market combine to make especial advantages for the dairyman.

As yet this section may not be as productive as older countries, for doubtless cultivation is not carried to as high a grade, but the capabilities are here, and each year our agriculturists are improving in their manner of cultivation, and the good effects are already being seen.

ADVERTISEMENT.—Through the hurry of urgent business, and from sheer unintentional inadvertence, the interim editors of the WORLD last week failed to think them on the entire Territorial Democratic ticket.

The name of our esteemed fellow townsman, Maj. K. Foote, should have appeared as a candidate for District Attorney for the Second Judicial District. A recent British journal thus discourses on a new process for cheapening the productions of steel by an American, of whom we know no more than is set forth in the article, wherefrom we extract as follows:


"THE SHERMAN PROCESS.—During the past few years, the ironmaking public has had brought before them so many processes for purifying iron manufacturing into steel, with less wonderful results that the advent of process, unless it be possessing more than merely claims to notice, has almost ceased to attract any general attention. Notwithstanding this, however, it is undoubted that there is still ample room for improvements in various methods of iron and steel making, and, particularly, there wanted means of turning to better account those cast irons produced in many districts among the many workers in this field. It is Mr. Edwin Sherman who has lately arrived in this country for the purpose of introducing his process, of which he is the inventor and with which, it is stated, successful results have already been obtained in America. Mr. Sherman has visited England at the invitation of our Government, conveyed through the British legation at Washington; earlier trials of his process made by him since his conducted &c. at the request of the Lords Commissioners of the Admiralty and partly under the supervision of one of their officers."


Why should this Mr. Sherman have found it necessary, or even advisable, to leave his own country in order to secure a fair trial of his process? Why should "the British legation at Washington" and the Lords Commissioners of the Admiralty take so much interest in an American invention, while no one in this country seems to have given any heed to it? Shall an American inventor never have a chance of consideration at home until he has secured the stamp of British appreciation? We know nothing of the value of this Sherman process, but regret that it had to cross the ocean for trial and judgment.


Codorus Ore, found near York, Pa., have been sent to and tested in Great Britain, with most satisfactory results. Mr. Sherman's process, we learn, consists of infusing a small quantity of certain cheap chemicals into the molten mass or bloom of pig iron, whereby certain deleterious minerals are eliminated, and the conversion of the mass into good steel rendered easy and certain. The Codorus Ore, being put into the furnace with the pig iron in the proportion of one to five, effects a like conversion, precipitating whatever phosphorus inheres in the metal and passing it off in the slag, and thus producing a choice steel for all uses at smaller cost than that of the Bessemer product whereof the uses are limited. Now we do not know that practical difficulties may not be encountered in working under the Sherman process or in using the Codorus Ore; but it seems to us that iron-masters generally should, as a rule, make themselves familiar with every such invention or discovery, with intent to utilize it if found available. Buying patents or discoveries is quite another matter; but whoever makes iron or steel should know all that is to be known with reference to his art, so as to be certain that he does not work to disadvantage when compared with his business rivals. We honor British legations and Lords Commissioners of the Navy for their attention to such matters; but we hope for a day wherein American inventors and discoveries will not need the patronage of either.

KING GEORGE COURT HOUSE, Va.

June 11, 1870.

William Taylor, condemned negro felon, executed fearful crime on the scaffold here to-day—a crime of triple nature, comprising murder, arson and robbery.

On the night of the 26th of March last, a shocking and atrocious tragedy was committed in this county. The circumstances were of the most appalling character and manifested on the part of the perpetrators a truly savage and brutal barbarism. On that night, in the lower part of the county, near a place called North Bend, on the Rappahannock river, a store, owned by a young merchant named F. W. Payne, was entered at the dead hour of midnight. The clerk, while Jett, a mere boy, was murdered, the store robbed and then, together with the body of the murdered boy, burned. Such an event, occurring in a peaceful neighborhood, produced a sensation like a thunderclap in a clear sky and the excitement throughout the country was intense. At early dawn a large crowd had assembled round the burned debris of the store, out of which the charred bones of the poor boy were taken. Everybody cried for vengeance; but yet no clue could be obtained as to the perpetrators of the foul deed.

ARREST OF THE PARTIES.

Soon, however, as murder will out, the damning evidences of guilt fastened suspicion on certain colored desperadoes living in the vicinity, and warrants were obtained for their arrest. A party was at once organized here, and, being well mounted, they started for the scene of the outrage. The officers and party arrived at the burned store in the afternoon and such disposition was at once made of the force to insure the capture of the robbers, and the houses of the suspected persons were searched, while another took a detour to the river bank in order to cut off the retreat of any who might attempt to escape. It was now night, and the avengers of blood had not long been in position when those at the river, in the shadow of the overhanging trees, discovered a boat paddling with muffled oars slowly down the river. It must be the boat which was hailed when about twenty yards distant. Upon this the men in the boat at once sprang into the river and began swimming for the opposite shore to escape capture. But their pursuers were not to be fooled. Two shots were fired at them from fowling pieces, but they still continued to swim. It was at this juncture it was feared they would escape under the cover of the darkness. With great intrepidity, however, Captain Spilman ran out into the river which, fortunately, was not deep, reached the boat into which he got, and called to the men, whose heads alone were above the water, to surrender, or he would shoot them down. As soon as the party at the houses heard the firing they rushed into the houses and a man ran past them who was shot at, but without effect, and he escaped in the darkness. They at once hastened to the river, and by their aid the two desperadoes who were endeavoring to escape were secured. These were found to be respectively William Taylor and Warren Taylor, both large athletic colored men, and noted desperate characters. So fearfully excited were some of the captors that it was with difficulty the officers could restrain them from passing upon William Taylor, Warren Taylor and George Miller.

The other man, who was shot at while running from one of the houses where the gang lived, was George Miller, a young negro thief, about seventeen years of age, frequent inmate of the county jail. In the boat was found several bags of merchandise of every variety usually to be found in a country store, which had been taken from the burned building. It was well known that others were implicated in the outrage and a search was made in all the houses which they had. They had to make a search of many miles through the heaviest easterly rain storm and darkest night ever experienced by any of them. By next day all the persons concerned in the dreadful act were apprehended and lodged in the jail here under charge of the keeper; the names of the prisoners being William Taylor and Reuben Hill. Upon examination it was found that both the men taken in the river were wounded, though not seriously; they at once received treatment and soon recovered. Soon afterwards two of the prisoners

CONFESSED

the crime. One of them, George Miller, the young negro, said that he and William Taylor went to the store after midnight; that he was in the habit of being there at all hours and was quite familiar with the little clerk, Jett. He found no difficulty in inducing the clerk to rise and light his lamp for the purpose of selling him a vial of oil for a sick child, he said. As soon as the door was open they rushed in and attacked Jett. Jett then fled through another door into the road, endeavoring to escape. He was pursued and beaten over the head with a gun until senseless or dying. He was then dragged into the store still breathing and left there. The murderers then went home for others to assist in carrying off the goods, and after taking all they wanted they saturated the door of the storeroom with kerosene oil and set it on fire. The store was situated in a place affording every opportunity for the preparation of such a crime.

THE TRIAL

of the criminals took place on the 5th of May before Judge J. B. Jett, recently elected, it being his maiden court. He had a stormy initiation. In addition to the seven culprits indicted for this crime there was a woman charged with infanticide, all of these malefactors being colored.

The evidence was full and convincing: for, besides the open admission of two of the murderers, there were other ample proofs. Commonwealth's Attorney T. G. S. Hunter conducted the prosecution with marked ability. Able lawyers were assigned by the court for the defence, and during the trial the courtroom was constantly crowded by an excited and angry crowd. William Taylor was sentenced to the penitentiary for a term of fourteen years. Warren Taylor and George Miller were sentenced to terms of eight years and Reuben Hill was acquitted. Since however, Governor Walker has commuted the sentence of George Miller on account of his youth to imprisonment for life in the penitentiary and he has respited Warren Taylor for sixty days.

Prior to the trial and conviction of these miscreants, a spirit of lawlessness and violence prevailed among the negroes in the entire section of the Northern Neck which culminated in this terrible crime. The arrest, summary trial and sentence, however, had a most salutary effect in restoring law and order; but since the commutation of the sentence of Miller and the respite of Warren Taylor, the negroes seem to be impressed with the idea that they are licensed to commit crime and outrage with impunity. To-day they did not pass upon William Taylor. Your correspondent was regarded by some of them as a special courier with the Governor's respite. On the other hand, the most intense feeling of indignation exists among the friends of the little murdered Jett, and, indeed, the entire community of whites, at the exercise of clemency towards Warren Taylor; and it was strongly intimated that he would be forcibly taken from the jail and lynched.

William Taylor,

THE CONDEMNED,

is a negro six feet high, broad shouldered, weighing about one hundred and seventy-five pounds, with a repulsive countenance, wearing the scowl of a savage and the contour of an animal in his expression; all the worst characteristics of the negro combined with the ferocity and strength of brute. Since his trial and sentence he has had little to say with regard to the triple crime he was the chief in perpetrating; but though never denying his guilt, he has insinuated there were others connected with it as yet unknown. Lately he became very penitent and last night he was seen with an expression of affection and fear. Every time he was visited he was found on his knees praying earnestly for salvation.

THE LAST NIGHT of his earthly existence was passed in restlessness and in prayer. This morning he was unable to partake of a special breakfast prepared by Mr. Rogers the sheriff. Merely drinking the coffee which he said made him feel better, he seemed in a more cheerful state of mind than for a number of days past.

ernment. They commence by saying that they

actually overthrown by certain laws recently
enacted by the Legislature now in session. The
petition closes as follows


All of our political rights have been taken
from us by our present Legislature and trans
ferred to the Executive of our State. We no
longer have the choice of our officers and
agents, but they are appointed over us by the
Executive. Strangers from other States igno-

law, are made Judges of our courts. Our civil
liberties have been destroyed, Republican gov
ernment has been overthrown in our State,

respectfully petition the Congress of the Uni
ted States to exercise its constitutional duty to
restore to this State Republican form of gov
ernment, and we do most solemnly appeal to
our fellow-citizens of the United States to aid
us in this our petition.
